meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The urge to destroy is also a creative urge'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Picasso. It's the last line of Mikhail Bakunin's 1842 essay 'The Reaction in Germany' — a paraphrase of the real translation, mis-credited to Picasso.

answer.label: Not Picasso — actually Mikhail Bakunin
answer.sourceLine: Pablo Picasso never wrote this. The line closes Bakunin’s 1842 essay “The Reaction in Germany,” whose standard English rendering is “The passion for destruction is a creative passion, too!” The familiar “urge to destroy… creative urge” wording is a later popular paraphrase, and the Picasso credit is a modern error — boosted when Banksy captioned his 2018 shredding stunt with the line “from Picasso.”

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: The Reaction in Germany (Die Reaktion in Deutschland. Ein Fragment von einem Franzosen)
October 1842, in Arnold Ruge’s Deutsche Jahrbücher für Wissenschaft und Kunst, under the pseudonym “Jules Elysard”
“The passion for destruction is a creative passion, too!” — popularly paraphrased as “The urge to destroy is also a creative urge.”

source.excerpt: Let us therefore trust the eternal Spirit which destroys and annihilates only because it is the unfathomable and eternal source of all life. The passion for destruction is a creative passion, too!
trail: The full text ends on the line “The passion for destruction is a creative passion, too!” in Bakunin’s 1842 essay “The Reaction in Germany” ↗, first published under the pseudonym Jules Elysard.
Wikiquote ↗ gives the sourced wording as “The passion for destruction is a creative passion, too!” and notes it is “often paraphrased as, ‘The urge to destroy is also a creative urge.’”
The Picasso credit spread widely after Banksy captioned his 2018 Sotheby’s shredding video with the line as “a… quote from Picasso,” per MyArtBroker ↗.
source.excerptNote: The closing lines of Bakunin’s essay, in the standard English translation. The “urge to destroy… creative urge” version widely pinned on Picasso is a loose paraphrase of this sentence.

sourceLink.text: Bakunin, “The Reaction in Germany” (1842) at Marxists.org

source.rightsNote: The line comes from Bakunin’s essay first published in October 1842; Bakunin died in 1876, so the original German text and its early English translations are long in the public domain in the United States. The specific popular one-liner is a loose modern paraphrase of that public-domain sentence rather than a distinct copyrighted work.

author.name: Mikhail Bakunin
author.heading: Who really wrote it
author.bio: Mikhail Bakunin was a Russian revolutionary and one of the founding theorists of collectivist anarchism, later Karl Marx’s great rival in the First International. The line closes his first major political essay, “The Reaction in Germany” (1842), written while he was a young Left Hegelian in Dresden. Its fusion of destruction and creation became a rallying cry for later radicals — famously resurfacing as graffiti in the 1968 Paris uprising.

copyAttribution: "The passion for destruction is a creative passion, too!" —Mikhail Bakunin, "The Reaction in Germany" (1842). Popularly paraphrased as "The urge to destroy is also a creative urge" and often misattributed to Pablo Picasso.

misattribution.heading: How it landed on Picasso
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s cleanest cases of a radical’s line being laundered into an artist’s aphorism. The thought is Bakunin’s; the Picasso tag is a 20th- and 21st-century invention.

items.why: Picasso was born in 1881 — five years after Bakunin died in 1876 — and the sentence predates him by nearly four decades, closing Bakunin’s 1842 essay “The Reaction in Germany” ↗. No Picasso text is ever cited as a source.
When Banksy’s “Girl with Balloon” self-shredded at Sotheby’s in October 2018, his video was captioned with the line as “a… quote from Picasso” — a caption seen by millions, per MyArtBroker ↗.

items.who: “The urge to destroy is also a creative urge”
items.why: The sourced translation is “The passion for destruction is a creative passion, too!” Wikiquote ↗ records the “urge to destroy” form explicitly as a paraphrase, not Bakunin’s (translator’s) exact words.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea — and the sentence — belong to Mikhail Bakunin’s 1842 essay “The Reaction in Germany” ↗, not to Pablo Picasso.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Bakunin wrote the essay in 1842 as a young Hegelian, and the closing line distills his lifelong conviction that tearing down old orders is itself an act of creation — the germ of the anarchism he would spend his life building.

The sentence outlived its author as a slogan: it reappeared as wall graffiti during the May 1968 revolt in Paris and, decades later, as Banksy’s caption for a self-destroying artwork — the moment that most firmly (and wrongly) welded it to Picasso’s name.
